activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: The method of loci is a memory trick of linking each part of a text to a place along a familiar route, then walking that route in your mind to recall it.
story:
Maya stood between the rows of headstones with her grandmother's prayer book open in her hands, and the pages flapped in the wind like they were trying to retire from the whole business. In three weeks she had to recite the entire reading at her coming-of-age ceremony, from memory, in front of everyone. She had tried repeating it at her desk, in the shower, on the bus, and every time she got to the fourth line the words dissolved like sugar in water.

"You're doing the mouth thing again," said Aarya, who was sitting cross-legged on the flat stone that marked the path. "Where you move your lips but nothing comes out."

"I'm practicing."

"You're panicking. Those are different."

Maya lowered the book. "Why are we even at a cemetery?"

"Because Harnoor said her aunt is buried here, and we're walking to her house after, and Ms. Shin is driving us, and Ms. Shin is visiting her brother's grave first." Aarya shrugged. "Also it's quiet. Good for your mouth thing."

Harnoor came back down the path with Ms. Shin, and Ms. Shin carried a small watering can and a paper bag of cut flowers. Maya watched her arrange them on one grave with careful, practiced hands.

"How do you remember where everything goes?" Maya asked. "Every flower, every week."

Ms. Shin smiled. "I've walked this path so many times I could do it with my eyes shut. Left at the tall angel, straight past the bench, second row from the oak."

Something clicked in Maya's head so hard she almost said ouch. Places. Her grandmother's house. She knew that house with her eyes shut too.

"Can we test something?" she said. She turned to the first line of the reading and imagined standing at her grandmother's front gate. The second line went on the porch step. The third, on the hook where the keys hung. The fourth, on the kitchen counter next to the fruit bowl.

"Now say them," said Harnoor, with heavy skepticism. "You put words on furniture. That's the most naive thing I've ever watched you do."

Maya closed her eyes. The gate. The porch step. The key hook. The fruit bowl. The words were just there, sitting in each spot like mail waiting to be opened. She said all four lines, then six, then ten, walking the whole house in her mind, past the humming fridge, up the creaky stair, all the way to the quilt on the spare bed.

"Okay," said Harnoor. "Okay, that's creepy. Do the next ten."

"It's got a name, I think," Maya said. "The method of loci. My cousin told me once. Each part of the text gets a place, then you walk the route in your head."

"Your brain is a haunted house now," said Aarya. "Congratulations."

Ms. Shin picked up her empty watering can. "Come on, then. We'll walk the long way, past the angel. You can hang a few more lines on it."

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: To ask for the bill in French, you say "L'addition, s'il vous plaît," meaning "The bill, please."
story:
Every summer Camille's grandmother spoke only French at the breakfast table, and every summer Camille pretended to understand more than she did. This year she had a plan. On Thursday she and her friend Leane, who was staying down the road, would walk to the little café on the square, and Camille would order lunch entirely in French, including asking what it cost, without pointing at the menu once.

They practised in the garden on Wednesday, while Leane, who wanted a perfect photo of a caterpillar for her nature project, knelt by the fennel and waited for a larva to do something interesting. "Je voudrais un croque-monsieur," Camille recited. "Combien ça coûte?" She had the ordering part down and the price part down. The bill part, she decided, was obvious. In English you ask for the note, so in French you would ask for la note. She even said it with a shrug, the way her grandmother did, and Leane said the shrug was more convincing than the accent.

At the café the next day, Camille ordered her croque-monsieur, and asked how much it cost, and the waiter answered all of it in rapid French that she caught about half of. So far, triumph. Then she made the mistake. When they finished eating, she raised her hand and said, "La note, s'il vous plaît." The waiter frowned, glanced at the table as if expecting to see a piece of paper with writing on it, and said something that included the word facture. Camille heard Leane take a breath beside her.

Camille did not want to resign herself to pointing at the menu or, worse, to English. She thought about it the way she thought about math problems. The waiter had understood everything else, so the problem wasn't her accent. The problem was the word. English borrowed note and facture meant invoice, so neither of those was the everyday café word. There had to be a third one, a word that meant the whole tally of the meal. She dredged up something her grandmother had muttered once at the kitchen table, tallying receipts after market day. "L'addition, s'il vous plaît," she tried.

The waiter's whole face changed. "Ah, l'addition, bien sûr," he said, and produced the bill as if he'd been waiting for the password all along. On the walk home, Leane scrolled through her photos and announced that the caterpillar had done nothing all afternoon except lie there. "Mine moved," Camille said. "It took me three tries, but it moved."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: An opinion supported with evidence is still an opinion, but it is a more convincing one than an opinion given with no reasons.
story:
Charles set his fork down and pulled his phone out of his pocket. His father had just said, for the third time, that the city was wasting money on a crosswalk for Halden Road. "Nobody uses that spot," his father said. "It's a desolate stretch of sidewalk. In my opinion, it's pointless."

"In your opinion," Charles said. He tapped the screen and held it up. On it was a message Simona had sent him that afternoon, and he read it aloud at the table. "Mr. Çelik had us do a traffic project, so I stood at Halden Road after school for four days. I counted fourteen near-misses, people stepping off the curb and jumping back. Fourteen. Also, Dexter fell in the mud doing it, so the crosswalk owes him a pair of shoes."

His father wiped his hands on his napkin and took the phone. He read the message twice, moving his lips a little on the second pass. "Fourteen near-misses," he said.

"That's evidence," Charles said. "She counted them. She wrote down the days and everything." He could feel himself leaning forward over his plate. "Doesn't that make her right?"

His father handed the phone back. "It makes her convincing," he said. "An opinion supported with evidence is still an opinion. It's just a more convincing one than an opinion given with no reasons." He picked up his fork again. "My no-reasons opinion is losing this round, I'll admit that."

Charles sat back. He had assumed the count settled things, that once you had numbers, the argument was over. His mother passed him the potatoes and said Simona should bring her list to the council meeting on Thursday. Charles said he would tell her, then ate quietly for a minute, thinking that his father had just handed him something better than a win. A rule. Numbers made you harder to argue with, but they did not turn you into a fact.

Thursday night, he went with Simona to the council meeting. She stood at the little podium with her handwritten chart, and when a council member asked how she knew the crosswalk was needed, she said, "Fourteen near-misses in four days. I counted them myself." Later, on the walk home, Dexter complained about his ruined shoes again, and Simona tried to console him by pointing out that his fall was now part of official public testimony. Dexter stopped on the corner, looked back at the council building, and said, "So my shoes are evidence too?"

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Antiperspirants reduce sweating by temporarily plugging sweat ducts, while deodorants do not stop sweat but reduce or cover the smell.
story:
The pharmacy smell hit George the moment the automatic doors slid open, a mix of cough drops and floor cleaner, and he walked straight to the aisle with the shelves of sticks and sprays. His problem was simple: yesterday, during the math test, sweat had soaked two gray crescents into his blue shirt, and Talia had leaned over and whispered, "Tide pool alert," which made Alyssa laugh so hard she got shushed by the teacher. His objective today was to make sure that never happened again.

He picked up a stick labeled DEODORANT and turned it over. The back said it reduced odor. It said nothing about sweat. He picked up the one next to it, labeled ANTIPERSPIRANT, and read that side too. This one said it reduced wetness. George frowned. He had assumed they were the same thing with different colors, the way two brands of the same cereal are basically the same cereal. Apparently not. One dealt with the smell, and the other dealt with the sweat itself. He was skeptical, though, because how could a smear of gel stop his armpits from doing what armpits do? He stood there comparing the labels, line by line, like a detective checking two suspects' alibis.

Last summer, before any of this mattered, he had gone with his dad to this same pharmacy for sunscreen, and they had stood in this same aisle while his dad grabbed whatever was cheapest. "You won't care about this stuff for years," his dad had said, ruffling his hair. George had believed him. Now he cared a lot, and he wondered if his dad had just forgotten what fourteen was like. Maybe the forgetting was part of being grown up, the way a mirror fogs in a steamy bathroom and the glass condenses into beads until you can't see your own face anymore.

"Deodorant or antiperspirant?" Talia asked. She had appeared at the end of the aisle, holding a birthday card, because of course the pharmacy was two blocks from school and of course she would find him here, holding armpit products up to the light.

"Antiperspirant," George said. "It stops the sweating. Deodorant only handles the smell."

"That's what my brother says too." She held up the card, which had a cartoon frog on it. "For Alyssa. You're coming Saturday, right? Because after the Tide Pool Incident, she feels bad about laughing, and she wants you there."

He hadn't known that. He looked at the antiperspirant in his hand, then at the shelf, and grabbed a second one.

"Two?"

"One for the locker," George said. "Emergency supply."

At the register, Mr. Tremblay from down the street was buying batteries, and he nodded at the sticks on the counter. "Smart," Mr. Tremblay said. "My boys fought that battle for years."

"Winning it now," said George, and put both sticks on the belt.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Gleaning is an ancient practice: the Book of Leviticus in the Hebrew Bible tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested for the poor and for strangers.
story:
The apples showed up again on Tuesday, six paper bags of them lined against the soup kitchen's back step, some of them bruised on one side, all of them perfectly good otherwise. Chase stacked them on the counter beside the oatmeal canisters and tried not to stare at the door. Monday there had been bags too, and Saturday before that, always before six in the morning, always without a note.

"Your guess is as good as mine," said the cook, chopping onions without looking up. "Been happening three weeks now."

Chase was there because his mother had signed him up, but the mystery had taken over. Somebody knew this door, knew when nobody was watching, knew exactly what the kitchen could use. He thought about it while he rinsed trays. A donor who wanted thanks would leave a card. A store dumping old stock would send it in crates with logos. These were plain bags, twist-tied by hand, and the bruised sides were always turned toward the wall, as if whoever left them didn't want anyone to feel embarrassed.

Yahya arrived at four with his grandmother, a small woman who sorted donated bread faster than anyone. Chase whispered his theory to Yahya at the sink. "I think it's one person, and I think they come on foot, because the bags are never wet even when the ground is. So they carry them under something. A coat, maybe." Yahya raised an eyebrow. "So test it."

Chase wrote a note and taped it to the step: "Thank you, whoever you are. You can knock. We're here at six." Then, because his math homework was due that afternoon, he worked through the formula for cylinder volume at the corner table while the last of the lunch crowd finished their soup. Outside the window, a flock of migratory geese went over, low and ragged, heading somewhere they knew without a map.

Next morning the note was gone and six new bags stood in its place, with one difference. On top of the apples sat a single sheet of paper, torn from a notebook, with one word penciled on it: "Leviticus." Chase frowned. He knew that was a book of the Bible, but nothing else.

Yahya's grandmother was slicing bread again. Chase held up the paper. "Do you know what this means?"

She smiled and dried her hands. "Gleaning," she said. "The Book of Leviticus in the Hebrew Bible tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested, for the poor and for strangers."

"So it's like that," Chase said slowly, the whole pattern clicking at once. "Leaving the good stuff where we'll find it. On purpose. Edges of the field, edge of the step." He ran out the back door into the alley, and there, half a block down, Mr. Bélanger from the corner grocery was walking away with empty bags folded under his coat. Chase didn't shout. He just held up the paper, and Mr. Bélanger raised one hand, quick, like a wave from a man who never meant to be seen.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Section 3 of the Canadian Charter gives every Canadian citizen the right to vote in elections for the House of Commons and provincial legislatures.
story:
Connor slid the pamphlet across the library table so fast it nearly flew off the edge. "Mr. Morningstar says we each have to explain one Charter right in our own words by Friday," he said. "I picked the voting one. Section three."

Tabitha leaned over, chewing her pen. "That's what I wanted. Find your own category." She flipped through her own pamphlet, hunting. "I've got mobility, whatever that means. Kelly has the language one."

"Because you can't just say 'voting is good,'" Kelly said, dropping into the third chair with a stack of sticky notes. "That's not explaining. My cousin tried that last year and got a C minus."

Connor stared at the page. The words were short but somehow slippery, like trying to hold water in a fist. "Okay, so it says something about the right to vote. But vote in what? That's the part I keep losing." He tapped the paper so hard it crumpled. "Maybe it's only federal stuff. Maybe municipal doesn't count. I speculate it's just the big national thing, since that's the one everybody talks about on TV."

"You're speculating wrong," Tabitha said. "Look further down the page."

He did, and there it was, plain as a doorbell. "Elections for the House of Commons and provincial legislatures," he read out loud. His chair scraped back as he stood. "Not municipal. The House of Commons and the provincial legislatures. And it's every Canadian citizen. It doesn't say every adult, it says every citizen. Wait." He grabbed a sticky note and wrote it down before the thought could leak away like air through the porous foam ball somebody had left dented on the shelf. "How do I check I've got it right, though? Like actually check?"

Kelly was already stuffing her notes in her bag. "The gym. The mock election. Mr. Morningstar set up the whole polling station thing for the grade eights, remember? There's a poster at the sign-in table about who can vote."

They half ran down the hall, sneakers squeaking. The gym smelled like floor wax and popcorn from the fundraiser, and along the far wall stood a folding table with a cardboard ballot box, a sign-in sheet, and a laminated poster. Connor planted himself in front of it and read every line twice, dragging his finger under the words.

"There." He pointed. "The poster says who can vote in a real federal election, and it matches. Canadian citizens only, eighteen and over in the elections law, but the Charter part, section three, gives every Canadian citizen the right to vote in elections for the House of Commons and provincial legislatures. That's the whole thing. I can say that in my own words without guessing."

"You're still guessing on one part," Tabitha said, squinting at the poster. "Because if the Charter says every citizen, does that include kids?"

Connor blinked. He read the poster again, lips moving. "It doesn't put an age on it," he said slowly. "So the Charter gives the right to every citizen, and the elections law is a different layer on top." He pulled out his sticky note and wrote one more line, then held it up. "Friday, I'm going to read this out and then ask the class exactly what Tabitha just asked me. Let them chew on it."

Kelly clapped him on the shoulder. "Better than a C minus."

"Way better," Connor said, and folded the note into his pocket like a winning ticket.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: A word problem can be turned into an equation: if a taxi charges 3 dollars plus 2 dollars per kilometre and a ride costs 15, then 3 + 2k = 15, so k = 6.
story:
The taxi receipt was still folded in Eva's pocket when she pushed through the door of the corner store, her grandmother two steps behind. Ms. Farah, who owned the place, was setting out a ballot jar for the student council vote, a pencil tied to the lid with string.

"Fifteen dollars," her grandmother said, tapping the receipt on the counter. "For a ride from the doctor's office. That seems wrong to me."

Eva smoothed the paper flat. "The card says three dollars plus two dollars per kilometre." She looked at the total again. "Fifteen."

"Can you work it out, or is that too trivial for you now?" her grandmother asked.

"It's not trivial," Eva said. "It's just, I don't know how far we went." Cruz came in behind them, shaking rain off his jacket, and leaned over the counter to look. Darwin followed, clutching a bag of chips he hadn't paid for yet.

Eva found a napkin and borrowed Ms. Farah's pencil. "It's three plus two times the kilometres," she said, and wrote 3 + 2k = 15. "We learned this on Tuesday. Whatever you do to one side, you do to the other side." She crossed out nothing; instead she wrote subtracting three from both sides, and the line below showed 2k = 12. Cruz craned his neck.

"Then divide both sides by two," Darwin said, through a mouthful of chips.

"I was getting there." She wrote k = 6. "Six kilometres. That's the ride."

Her grandmother took the napkin and studied it. "Six. I thought it was more like four."

"Six," Eva said. "Every kilometre is two dollars, plus three to start. Fifteen total means six."

Ms. Farah slid the ballot jar toward them. "Since you three are here, cast your votes before Friday. And put that draft of yours somewhere better than the floor," she added, nodding at the crumpled poster that had slipped from Cruz's bag, the one that read CRUZ FOR TREASURER in marker gone over twice.

Cruz smoothed the poster against the counter and dropped his folded ballot into the jar. "Six kilometres," he said to Eva. "You just figured out something you couldn't see. That's the whole ride, from a number on a receipt."

Eva folded the napkin along the crease she'd made and tucked it into her pocket next to the receipt. "Grandma, on the way home, count the blocks."

"I will," her grandmother said, and picked up her bag. "And if I count wrong, you'll fix that too."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: The lines that run back toward the vanishing point are called orthogonals, and in a street scene they include road edges, curbs and rooflines.
story:
Dominic stood in the corner of the community gallery where Ms. Chea had set up drawing tables beside a tall window. On the wall hung a painting of a narrow street, and she had told everyone to choose a painting and copy its bones. "Draw your orthogonals first," she said, walking past his table. "Everything else comes after." Dominic stared at his blank page. He had no idea what she meant, but he wasn't going to ask in front of Vada, who was already halfway through her sketch of a stone bridge.

He looked back at the street painting. Somewhere deep in the picture, the road seemed to shrink to a single point, like a street seen down a microscope where even a microbe of distance swallowed everything. He laid his pencil ruler across the canvas and tried to see which lines in the painting actually pointed at that spot. The two edges of the road, obviously. He tested them with his ruler, and yes, both ran straight toward the shrinking point. Then he tried the curbs, holding the ruler up like a tiny tightrope, and those ran back toward it too.

"Are you measuring the painting with your ruler?" Vada whispered. "That looks a little crazy."

"Give me one minute," Dominic said. He looked higher. The roofs of the buildings on either side, sloped back and inward, and when he laid the ruler along a roofline, it aimed at the same distant point. So did the line of awnings. Every line that ran back into the distance seemed to share one destination. He copied the road edges first, then the curbs, then the rooflines, all of them converging on a dot he marked faintly in the middle of his page.

Alexi leaned over from the next table. "Why did you do the rooftops before the doors and windows?"

"Because those are the lines that run back toward the vanishing point," Dominic said. "The road edges, the curbs, the rooflines. Apparently those have a name. Orthogonals." He said the word slowly, testing it. "Ms. Chea said it. I just figured out which lines she meant."

Ms. Chea stopped behind him and looked at his page, at the clean fan of lines meeting at their dot. She nodded once and moved on. Dominic began to anticipate what would come next, the windows and doors that would slot between his lines like teeth, and he drew the first window, then another, each one smaller than the last, marching down the street toward the dot.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: A control group in an experiment gets everything the test group gets except the thing being tested, so any difference between the groups can be linked to that one thing.
story:
Sadie slid her two bean pots onto the counter at the back of the science classroom and frowned at them. Both plants had sprouted, both had tall green stems, and both looked exactly as healthy as the other. She had added fertilizer to one pot every Friday for three weeks, and she had been so sure that pot would tower over the other one by now. Maddex leaned over her shoulder and whistled. "They're twins," he said. "So much for your fertilizer."

"I can't postpone the science fair, either," Sadie said. "It's Thursday." The problem gnawed at her all through Mr. Kapoor's opening announcements. If both plants looked the same, she couldn't claim the fertilizer worked. But she also couldn't claim it didn't work, because something felt wrong, and she couldn't say what.

Then, during the warm-up question, she looked at her pots again and saw it. She had given the fertilized plant everything the other plant got, plus the fertilizer, but the two pots weren't identical. The fertilized one sat by the window, where the sun poured in all afternoon. The other one sat on the shelf in the corner. The unfertilized plant had less light, and it had caught up anyway. She raised her hand so fast she nearly knocked over Gurshaan's water bottle. "Mr. Kapoor, can I move my pots? Both of them, same spot, side by side."

"Of course," he said, and turned back to the board.

She carried the pots to the window and set them flush against each other, then labeled them A and B. "Now the one without fertilizer gets everything A gets except the fertilizer," she told Gurshaan, who had wandered over. "Same light, same water, same dirt. That's called a control group." Gurshaan nodded slowly. "So if A pulls ahead now," he said, "you'll know it's the fertilizer and not the window." Sadie grinned. Exactly that.

Maddex came back at lunch, looked at the pots in their new spot, and shook his head. "I thought you were proving the fertilizer works," he said. "Now you're just starting over." "Not over," Sadie said. She watered both plants with the same careful pour, the same amount in each pot. "Just honest. If A wins now, I'll know why. And if it doesn't, I'll know that too." She wrote the day's date on a fresh data sheet and clipped it to the window frame, right between the two pots, where she couldn't miss it tomorrow morning.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: The piano's full name is pianoforte, meaning soft-loud, because the player can make notes soft or loud by how hard the keys are struck.
story:
George sat at the piano in the living room with the sheet music for "Moonrise" open on the stand, and for the third time that afternoon he played the loud part too loud and the soft part not soft enough. The mp at measure twelve was supposed to shrink the sound, and the ff at measure twenty was supposed to swell, but everything came out the same size, like the notes were wearing identical shoes. His mother had accused him last night of "banging," and she wasn't wrong. He pressed the keys with his whole arm, the way he pressed the heavy door at school, and the piano just made one big sound after another.

He tried again and watched his own hands. What if the difference wasn't in his fingers at all, but in how hard each key was struck? He laid one finger on middle C and let it sink slowly. A small, round note floated out, thin as vapor rising off a mug of cocoa. Then he struck the same key harder, and the note bloomed, warm and full, like molten gold poured into a mold. Same key. Same finger. Different weight.

By the window, Diana looked up from the book she'd been pretending to read for twenty minutes. "It's called a pianoforte, you know," she said. "Soft-loud. That's the whole name. The player can make notes soft or loud by how hard the keys are struck."

"That's why the pedal in my book says forte here and piano there," George said. "It's not telling me where to bang. It's telling me how to weigh each key." He went back to measure twelve and this time he let his fingers fall like leaves, and the melody dropped to a whisper that made Diana lean forward to hear it. At measure twenty he pressed through the keys with weight instead of hitting them, and the sound rose up big and round without a single harsh edge.

He played the whole piece through once, then again, and the second time the quiet part actually felt quiet and the loud part felt like it had earned its place. "Do it once more," Diana said, closing her book. "And this time do that soft bit at the end like you're lowering it into a drawer."

George set his hands on the keys and began.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: The saying that compound interest is 'the eighth wonder of the world' is often credited to Albert Einstein, but there is no reliable evidence he ever said it.
story:
Georgia spread two posters across the kitchen table, one labelled SIMPLE and one labelled COMPOUND. She had promised Mr. Ba's class a five-minute presentation on which kind of savings account would earn more over five years, and she had worked the numbers so many times they practically orbited in her head. Simple interest paid the same amount every year, like a machine dropping one coin at a time. Compound interest paid interest on the interest, and by year five the gap had grown wide enough to surprise her. She tapped the compound poster with her pencil and said out loud, "Why does it work like that? You can't even see it happening."

She had saved the best part for last, a quote she'd found online: "Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world," attributed to Albert Einstein. It would make a perfect ending. She wrote it at the bottom of the poster in her best handwriting, then paused. Mr. Ba had a rule he repeated like a drumbeat: check your sources. Would Einstein really have said something like that? It felt odd, like finding out your math teacher wrote poetry about money.

Georgia opened her laptop and searched for where the quote came from. The first sites just repeated it. She dug further, into library pages and quote archives, and the picture turned murkier than the poster. The saying was often credited to Einstein, but there was no reliable evidence he ever said it. She sat back. Something that famous, and nobody could prove it? It was a little sinister, like a rumour wearing a lab coat.

The phone buzzed. Johnny had texted: "Did you finish? Katelynn says end on the Einstein thing." Georgia typed back, "The Einstein thing might be fake. Checking one more time." She found a reference librarian's answer page, then a second one saying the same thing, and after that she believed it. She crossed out the attribution on her poster and wrote instead, "Often credited to Einstein, but no reliable evidence he said it."

The next morning she stood at the front of the room with both posters taped to the board. She walked the class through year one, year three, year five, showing how compound pulled ahead. "And here's the strangest part," she said. "The most famous quote about compound interest is usually credited to Einstein, but there's no reliable evidence he ever said it." Mr. Ba raised his eyebrows and nodded slowly. Katelynn's hand shot up. "So who said it?" Georgia grinned. "Nobody knows. I think that's almost as interesting as the math." Johnny leaned over his desk and whispered, "Nice save on the poster."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed in the Great Vowel Shift after spellings had started to become fixed, which is a major reason English spelling often doesn't match pronunciation.
story:
Bentley spread the word list across the kitchen table and stared at "bite" like it had personally insulted him. "Why is there an e? It doesn't do anything. It just sits there."

Archer leaned over from the counter, where he was making popcorn for the third time because the first two batches burned. "It does do something. It makes the i say its name."

"Then why not spell it like it sounds?" Bentley flipped the page. "B-I-T-E. And then there's 'knife.' Who decided the k stays?"

Ewan, sprawled on the couch with his feet on the armrest, lowered his phone. "The spelling bee is Saturday. Maybe stop arguing with the dictionary."

Bententley couldn't stop, though. The list for the regional qualifier had forty words, and half of them seemed designed to trick him. He needed to be systematic about it, so he had made three columns: words that sounded like they looked, words that didn't, and words he honestly couldn't tell. The middle column was the longest by far. He tried to assess which ones would actually trip him up, and the pattern he found was strange. The weird ones weren't random. Long vowels were the worst. "Bite," "meet," "stone," "wife." All of them had letters sitting around doing nothing.

He went looking for an answer himself, in the dusty reference books his mom kept on the shelf above the television. The third one he opened had a chapter on the history of English, and there it was. He read the paragraph twice, then carried the book to the couch and held it out to Ewan.

"Listen to this. Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed. It's called the Great Vowel Shift."

"Sounds like a dance move," Ewan said, but he took the book.

"And here's the part that makes me want to flip this table. The spellings had already started to become fixed before the shift happened. So people wrote down words one way, then everybody started saying them differently, and nobody went back to fix the spelling. That's why English spelling often doesn't match pronunciation. It's not that the letters are lying. It's that the sounds moved and the letters stayed home."

Archer came over with the popcorn, reading over Bentley's shoulder. "Wait, three hundred years of people just... talking differently?"

"Apparently."

"So 'bite' used to sound more like 'beet,'" Ewan said slowly.

Bentley looked at his list again, and the middle column suddenly looked less like enemies and more like fossils. Each silent e was a mark left by a sound that had wandered off centuries ago. He felt an odd sympathy for the old spellings, the way you might feel empathy for someone left standing at a bus stop after the bus already left.

On Saturday, Mr. Hamdan from next door came over to watch, since the qualifier was online and each family needed an adult present to confirm no cheating. He settled into the chair by the window with his tea. The pronouncer's voice came through the speakers, tinny but clear.

"Your word is 'quiet.'"

Bentley closed his eyes. Long i, and the e after the t. A sound that had shifted, and the spelling that had stayed behind, waiting. He could see the word the way a person in 1400 might have said it.

"Q-U-I-E-T. Quiet."

"Correct."

Archer whooped and knocked over the popcorn bowl. Mr. Hamdan raised his teacup like a toast. "Six more to go, Bentley," he said. "Take us back to the fifteenth century."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: A 2001 study of school playgrounds found that when a classmate stepped in to stop bullying, the bullying stopped in more than half of the cases.
story:
Adam sat cross-legged on Addisyn's basement floor, holding a lump of gray clay that felt like a cold sponge. "My uncle's an artisan," Addisyn said, shaping her own lump into a bowl. "He says good clay is porous, so water seeps out slowly while it dries. That's why his bowls don't crack." Adam pressed his thumb into the clay and watched the dent stay, which made him wonder how something so soft could ever become a hard bowl. He was about to ask when the doorbell rang.

It was Brandon, from their history class, carrying his project materials in a plastic bag. Addisyn had invited him because he was the only one who knew how to make a proper glaze, but the moment he saw her bowl, he laughed. "That looks like a mashed potato with a dent in it. Were you trying to make a bowl or a hat for a hamster?"

Addisyn's shoulders went stiff. She set the bowl down and pretended to be busy with the clay bag, but her ears had gone pink, and she didn't say anything back. Adam glanced at her, then at Brandon, who was grinning and waiting for a reaction. Adam's first instinct was to say "Brandon, you're being a jerk," but he had tried that once at lunch last year, and it had turned into a shouting match that got them both detention while the teasing found a new target. So how did stepping in actually work?

He thought about a poster in the school library that he'd read while waiting for the computer lab to open. It described a 2001 study of school playgrounds, and one line had stuck with him: when a classmate stepped in to stop bullying, the bullying stopped in more than half of the cases. More than half. That meant a kid like him, just saying something, worked most of the time. But the poster hadn't said what to say, and Adam suspected the how mattered. Maybe a kid who stepped in with an insult made things worse, while a kid who stepped in and changed the direction of the moment made things better. He decided to test it right there, on the clay.

"Brandon," Adam said, holding up his own lump, which honestly looked like a raccoon had sat on it, "you're the glaze expert, so judge mine. Does this count as modern art or a crime scene?" Brandon squinted at it and laughed. "That's a crime scene." "Right?" Adam said. "Addisyn's bowl is at least recognizable. Mine looks like it lost a fight with itself." Addisyn snorted, and some of the stiffness went out of her shoulders.

Brandon ended up demonstrating glaze on Adam's crime scene, and by the time Addisyn's bowl came out of the little kiln, lopsided but whole, he was showing her how to fix the rim on the next one. Adam watched them and wondered whether the poster's numbers were about this exactly, a moment bent just slightly off its track. Maybe, he thought, standing up for someone wasn't about winning a fight at all. He rolled his clay into a ball and held it up. "Okay, expert. Bowl, hat, or hamster?"

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: A spreadsheet cell's address is its column letter followed by its row number, so C4 is the cell in column C, row 4.
story:
Sydney sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with the laptop balanced on a stack of textbooks, because her desk had vanished under three weeks of laundry. The assignment was due Monday: a spreadsheet of world animal populations, a formula that added a column, and a bar chart. Mr. Santos had shown the class one example on Friday, then closed the projector and said, "You'll figure it out." Sydney had not figured anything out yet.

She typed her numbers into column B, one animal per row. Amur leopards, 100. Vaquita porpoises, 10. Sumatran rhinos, fewer than 80. Some of these animals would be extinct within her lifetime, and that thought had made her choose them in the first place, when the topic of endangered species had started a controversial argument in class and Jaycee had said saving ten porpoises was a waste of money. Sydney wanted a chart so clear that nobody could argue with it.

The formula defeated her twice, so she called Benjamin, who had finished his spreadsheet on Saturday. "Type equals, then SUM, open paren," he said over the phone, his mouth full of something crunchy. "Then B2 colon B11, close paren, enter."

She typed it. The cell at the bottom of her list showed 3,904. But that number seemed too big. Her biggest group was 1,000 whooping cranes, and everything else was small. She added the column by hand on paper and got 2,904. A thousand animals had appeared out of nowhere.

"Benjamin, check my formula," she said. "Read me exactly what's in B12."

He read it back: "SUM, C2 to C11."

"There's your problem," Sydney said slowly, staring at the screen. The numbers ran down column B, but the column beside it, column C, was where she'd typed each animal's continent. Africa, Asia, Asia. And in row 4, she had typed a number by mistake, a note she'd made about breeding programs: 1000. The formula hadn't invented a thousand animals. It had gone one column to the right and found her own note sitting in C4.

"How do you even know that?" Benjamin asked.

"Because C4 means column C, row 4," Sydney said. "Look at the edges. Letters across the top, numbers down the side. It's like a map." She fixed the formula, watched 2,904 appear, and felt something click into place that hadn't been there before.

She highlighted the animal names and the counts, clicked Insert Chart, and the bars jumped up on the screen. The whooping crane bar towered over everything, and at the very bottom, barely a sliver, sat the vaquitas. Ten. The bar was almost invisible, which was the whole point, because that thin line was a whole species.

Sydney screenshotted it and sent it to Jaycee with one message: "Ten left. Argue with the chart."

Then she sat back and looked at that smallest bar until her phone buzzed on the carpet beside her knee.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: According to the USDA, a refrigerator keeps food safely cold for about four hours during a power cut, as long as its door stays closed.
story:
The lights went out at her grandmother's house just after seven, while Laurence was helping dry the dishes. From the kitchen window she could see that the whole street was dark, porch lights and all, so the trouble was somewhere beyond the house. Her grandmother felt her way to the junk drawer and found a candle, and Melanie, who had come over to work on their science project, lit it with a shaking match.

"Grand-maman, stop," Laurence said, because her grandmother had already opened the refrigerator and was peering in at the shelves. "Every time you open it, the cold gets out."

"There's cheese in there, and yogourt," her grandmother said. "It will spoil."

Laurence closed the door and stood in front of it like a guard. Last summer, during the power cut at her own house, she had opened the fridge maybe six times hunting for a snack, and by morning the milk had gone sour. She had felt bad about that for weeks, and she still wasn't sure whether the milk had spoiled because of her or whether it would have gone anyway. She wasn't going to let it happen twice without finding out. She found her phone in the dark and typed in her question, and the answer came back on the dim screen. "It says a fridge keeps food safely cold about four hours during a power cut," she read aloud, "as long as the door stays closed."

"Four hours," her grandmother repeated. "Then we can have the cheese later."

Melanie, who was writing everything down for the science project because she liked being explicit about her data, printed FOUR HOURS in large letters on a napkin. She asked if the seeds they had left in the garage would be all right without heat, and Laurence said seeds just sit there until conditions are right; they germinate when it's warm and wet, so a cold night would only keep them waiting, not hurt them.

They moved to the living room with the candle and played cards by its small circle of light. When the lights came back on at nine, her grandmother reached for the fridge handle, but Laurence caught her wrist. "Not yet. It's only been two hours. We open it once, so decide everything you want first." Her grandmother laughed and made her list: cheese, milk, the leftover soup. Only then did they open the door together, and the cold air rolled out over their hands.

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: In the 2005 United Kingdom general election, Labour won a majority of seats with 35.2 percent of the vote.
story:
Chase had come to his grandpa's house expecting to help renovate the garden shed, not to argue about elections. But the rain hammered down, so the two of them sat at the kitchen table with cocoa, and Grandpa pulled out an old newspaper clipping he kept folded inside a recipe book.

"School project?" Grandpa asked, tapping the page where Chase had scrawled his homework title, "Voting Systems." Chase groaned. He had to compare first-past-the-post with something called proportional representation, and he only half understood either one. He said the words aloud and they slid off him like water off the shed roof they were supposed to be fixing.

Grandpa laughed and fetched a bag of buttons from the junk drawer. He dumped them out. "Say these are voters." He divided them into clumsy heaps. "Forty red, thirty blue, twenty green, ten yellow. Ten seats up for grabs. Under proportional representation, how would you split the seats?" Chase counted on his fingers. Four, three, two, one. It felt fair, almost tidy. Then Grandpa drew ten tall rectangles on a sheet of paper and said they were districts, and told Chase to spread the voters however he liked across them. Chase started sorting, then stopped, staring.

"Wait," he said. "If I put the reds evenly, they win almost everywhere." He spread them out, district by district, and the reds took seat after seat while the blues piled up in two districts and the greens and yellows got nothing. He leaned back. "Red gets most of the seats. But red doesn't even have half the voters." He checked his own numbers twice, because it seemed like a trick. It wasn't. It was just what happened.

Grandpa stirred his cocoa and looked out at the rain. "I lived in Britain for years," he said. "In the 2005 United Kingdom general election, Labour won a majority of seats with 35.2 percent of the vote." Chase wrote that down carefully, then looked at his buttons. About a third of the votes, most of the seats. His spread-out reds had done the same thing. He couldn't see the rule, exactly, because it wasn't a thing you could hold, but he could see what it did, over and over, every time he dealt the voters out again.

When Nova texted to ask if he'd finished the project, Chase texted back, "Getting there. Found out the weird part with buttons." Then Grandpa stood, wincing at his knee, and Chase noticed the roof bucket in the hall was nearly full. He carried it to the sink and emptied it before it could overflow, because Grandpa had been so busy helping him he'd forgotten to check. "Wouldn't want to be negligent about my own leak while I'm teaching you politics," Grandpa said. Chase grinned, dealt the buttons out one more time, and slid the sheet across the table. "You're blue," he said. "Pick your districts."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: Copying =SUM(B2:B10) one column to the right turns it into =SUM(C2:C10), because ordinary cell references are relative and shift with the formula.
story:
The office smelled like burnt coffee, and Alex had three hours to kill while his mom finished her meeting. On her desk sat a sticky note in her handwriting: "Data on the desktop. Do not touch. Back at 4."

He touched it immediately, obviously, because he needed to make a bar chart for science class and his laptop was at home. Gabriella had sent him a message that morning, and he read it again on his phone: "Mr. Domenic bet me a smoothie your chart looks terrible. Prove him wrong. G."

The file was a list of seedling growth for the school greenhouse project, ten rows of numbers under a column labeled Week 1, then more columns, Week 2 through Week 5. Ms. Johansson, who worked at the desk beside his mom's, leaned over and said, "Type =SUM(B2:B10) in the box below the first column. That adds the whole thing."

He typed it, hit enter, and the total appeared like magic: 84. One column down. But there were five more columns, and his mom would be back at four, and Domenic's smug face floated in his imagination like a bad omen.

"Unless you want to type it five more times," Ms. Johansson said, grinning, "copy that cell and paste it into the next one over."

Alex copied the formula, pasted it one column to the right, and then froze. The number that appeared was not 84. It was 91, which was exactly the total of the second column, Week 2. He stared at the screen. He had pasted the same formula. How could the same formula give a different number?

His first idea was that the program had made a mistake. He clicked the pasted cell, and there in the formula bar it did not say =SUM(B2:B10) anymore. It said =SUM(C2:C10). He pasted it into the next column and checked again: =SUM(D2:D10). The formula was moving with him.

"So they're relative," Ms. Johansson said, peeking at his screen. "Relative references. They shift with the formula."

He dragged the little square at the corner of the cell all the way across the row, and every column total appeared at once, like dominoes falling. His extinct excuse of "my computer is broken" would never work again. The bar chart took two clicks after that, bars climbing from Week 1 to Week 5 like the seedlings themselves, which the greenhouse club had worked all spring to nurture.

At 3:58 his mom's office chair was still empty. Alex screenshotted the chart, texted it to Gabriella, and typed: "Tell Domenic to bring the smoothie. Extra large."

The reply buzzed back within seconds: "He says 'no fair, you had professional help.' Enjoy your victory."

Alex leaned back, spinning slowly in his mom's chair, and hit print.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In the 2020 NFL season, when most games had few or no fans because of COVID-19, home teams finished 127-128-1, showing no significant home advantage.
story:
The living room was so crowded that Jayden had to share the good spot on the couch with Harris, while Alayna sat on the floor with her back against the coffee table. Mr. Luo from next door had brought a bowl of popcorn, and Dad had hung a paper banner over the TV that said GO GO GO in letters so big they looked almost sinister. The home team was losing by four points with six minutes left, and everybody was yelling.

"They play better when we're loud," Dad insisted, pounding the armrest. "Home crowd wins games. That's the whole point of home field."

Jayden wasn't so sure. He thought about the story his uncle had told him at Thanksgiving, about the 2020 NFL season, when almost nobody was allowed in the stadiums because of COVID-19. His uncle had said the home teams that year finished 127-128-1, which meant they lost exactly as many as they won. If screaming fans were what made home field matter, that season should have been a disaster for home teams. It wasn't. "So maybe the crowd doesn't actually do anything," Jayden said out loud.

"That's crazy," Harris said, spraying popcorn crumbs. "Watch. When we cheer, they move the ball. When we go quiet, they stall."

"That could be luck," Jayden said. "You're only counting the times it fits." He grabbed the notepad Alayna kept in her backpack for drawing. "We can test it. Next two drives. We cheer like maniacs for one drive, then we go totally silent for the other, and we write down what happens either way."

Alayna grinned and drew a chart with two columns. "What's the criterion?" she asked. "Like, what counts as a good drive?"

"First down or more," Jayden said. "If they get a first down, that drive gets a check."

Drive one, the whole room roared. They stomped, they chanted, Mr. Luo waved a dishtowel like a flag, and the crowd noise on the TV itself portrayed a stadium in chaos. The home team went three and out. Dad looked personally betrayed.

Drive two, silence. It was the hardest thing Jayden had ever done, sitting on his hands while the quarterback dropped back. Alayna held her breath so hard her cheeks bulged. The silence lasted one play, two, and then a third-down pass sailed forty yards down the sideline, and the receiver tiptoed in at the pylon. First down, and the whole room exploded anyway, because nobody could help it.

"So the silent drive was better," Alayna said, marking the chart, her voice squeaky with laughing.

"One test doesn't prove anything," Jayden said. "That's what my uncle always says. You'd need a whole season."

Dad leaned over and studied the notepad. "Fine," he said, holding up the popcorn bowl like a peace offering. "But until the season's over, we yell anyway."

"Deal," said Harris, with his mouth already full.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: A mirror ball turns one spotlight into hundreds of moving spots of light because each small mirror tile reflects the beam in a slightly different direction.
story:
Nathaniel stood in the hallway outside the gym with his tie stuffed in his pocket, listening to the bass thump through the double doors. The dance started in ten minutes, and he had promised Cecily he would walk in with her, which was easy to promise on Tuesday and terrifying to do on Friday. He adjusted his shirt collar in the small mirror outside the science room, next to a poster about fungi that read "Decomposers break down leaves into nutritious soil." He could perceive his own nerves in the mirror, in the way his mouth kept pressing into a flat line.

Cecily arrived with Ayva, both of them glittery, and Cecily had her own problem. "I want to dance under the mirror ball," she said, "at least once, before the night ends. But everybody crowds the middle, and I can't figure out where to stand so the spots actually land on you." Ayva shrugged. "Just push in there." "I don't push," Cecily said, with dignity.

Mr. Luo unlocked the doors early, and Nathaniel drifted in after the girls, glad for a reason to move. Above the empty dance floor hung the mirror ball, still dark, waiting for the spotlight that the janitor would switch on when the music started. Nathaniel had never looked at one up close before. It was not one big mirror. It was hundreds of tiny mirror tiles, every one glued on at its own angle, each one tilted a little differently from its neighbor.

"So that's it," he said aloud. Cecily and Ayva came over. "Watch," he said. "There's one spotlight, but each tile reflects the beam in a slightly different direction. That's why you get all those moving spots sweeping the floor. One light, hundreds of little mirrors." Ayva frowned. "You can't know that." "I can test it," Nathaniel said. He cupped his hand in front of the janitor's lamp where it sat on its stand, angled up, and wiggled one finger across the front of the beam. On the far wall, a whole patch of tiny spots shivered at once, like startled fish.

"It's one spot times hundreds," Cecily said slowly, following the sweep of light with her eyes. "So the spots travel together, in a pattern." She walked to the edge of the floor and stood where the beam pointed, then traced its path across the tiles with her finger, and stepped three paces left. "When the music starts, the spots will come through here," she said. "Every rotation. I timed the ball turning." Ayva checked her watch. "Two minutes till the doors open."

The music came up, the lamp snapped on, and the ball began to turn. Spots spilled across the gym in slow, circling rivers, and just as Cecily had predicted, a river of them crossed her three paces left. She grabbed Nathaniel's sleeve and pulled him into the light, and the little mirrors scattered brightness over them both while Ayva stood at the edge grinning and shouting, "You two look like a couple of fireflies!"

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Smokey Bear's campfire rule is drown, stir, drown again, then feel for heat, because if a campfire is too hot to touch, it is too hot to leave.
story:
Jade had saved for two summers from dog-walking income to pay for a week at Camp Wyoka, and now that she was actually here, she was lying awake on the top bunk listening to Beckett snore and wishing she hadn't spent a single dollar.

The trouble had started at the evening campfire. Their cabin group had roasted marshmallows by the fire ring near the lake, and when it was time for bed, the counselor had dumped water on the flames until nothing glowed. Jade had been the last one to leave. She kept thinking about a curl of smoke she thought she'd seen rising from the ashes after everyone turned away, thin as thread, there and then gone. Maybe she'd imagined it. Wind moved everything at this camp, branches and shadows alike.

"It's out," Beckett had said when she mentioned it on the walk back. "Drowned. Done. Worrying about it isn't logical." Augustus had agreed, half asleep already, and Jade hadn't argued, because what did the new kid know anyway?

But at two in the morning, she decided the new kid could still be right. She climbed down without a sound and shook Augustus's shoulder. "Come check the fire ring with me. Two minutes." He groaned, sat up, and pulled on his shoes. At the door, Beckett's voice came out of the dark. "Wait. I'm coming too. If there's a fire, I'm not lying here wondering."

The ring of stones looked cold and dead, exactly as they'd left it. "See?" Beckett whispered. Jade crouched and held the back of her hand above the ashes, then lowered it slowly. Heat. Not much, but real, like a kettle three rooms away. "It's still warm," she said. Augustus knelt beside her and felt it too. "So what do we do?"

"More water," Jade said. There was a bucket by the water pump, and she filled it and poured it over the pit until the ashes hissed and steamed. Then she grabbed a stick and stirred the whole mess, turning up coals from underneath, because if she'd learned one thing from the flyer in the camp office, it was that you drown it, stir it, drown it again, and then you feel for heat. She said the words out loud so she wouldn't forget them, and Beckett repeated them back like a chant while he stirred.

After the second bucket, Jade held her hand over the pit, lower and lower. It felt like nothing at all, like the ground anywhere. "If a fire's too hot to touch, it's too hot to leave," she said, standing up. "This one we can leave."

They walked back under the stars, and Beckett put an arm around her shoulders. "Okay," he admitted. "You were right and I was wrong, and I'm glad you woke us up." In the morning they'd tell the counselor, and maybe Jade would tell her mom it had been a good week after all. Beckett pointed at the sky. "Look, a shooting star."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In one-point perspective, all lines going straight back into the distance meet at a single vanishing point on the horizon line, at the viewer's eye level.
story:
Lucas tapped his pencil against the edge of the art room table and stared at the photograph pinned to the easel in front of him. It showed the main road from his summer camp, running straight back between two rows of pine trees until the asphalt narrowed to a sliver. Mr. Grewal had assigned the whole class a street scene in one-point perspective, and Lucas had assumed that meant drawing a road with edges that angled inward. His first attempt lay flat on the table, and something about it looked wrong in a way he could not name.

Daxon leaned over from the next stool, chewing the end of his own pencil. "Yours looks like the road is folding in half," he said.

"Thanks a lot." Lucas held the sketch at arm's length. "The weird part is my buildings look fine but the road looks like a ramp. And the sidewalk doesn't match either." He had drawn the left edge of the road toward the left side of the paper, the right edge toward the right, and the sidewalk lines somewhere in between, each heading to its own imaginary point. Three directions, three guesses. It was almost logical, in the way a stick figure is almost a person.

Mia slid her chair around and set her sketchbook down beside his. She had been quiet all period because she wanted hers finished first, finished best, finished before anyone could offer advice. "Maybe the road edges are supposed to aim at the same place," she said, keeping her eyes on her own paper. "Look at the photo. Follow one edge with your finger."

Lucas laid his finger along the left edge of the road in the photograph, then traced the right edge. Somewhere near the middle of the picture, both lines seemed to run together, along with the sidewalk lines and even the edges of the distant treeline. "They're all going to the same spot," he said slowly. "Like they're being pulled in."

"That's the vanishing point," Mia said.

He checked her tone for smugness and found none, just hurry, because she had already moved on to her own drawing. Lucas grabbed a fresh sheet. First he drew a horizontal line across the middle for the horizon, then a single dot sitting on it. He remembered Mr. Grewal mentioning eye level offhandedly last week, something about how the horizon sat where your eyes were, and now the pieces fit together. The dot had to sit on that line. He ruled lines from the dot outward, like sunbeams, and let the edges of his road ride two of them into the distance.

"Wait," Daxon said, peering over. "Even the sidewalks? And the building edges?"

"Everything that goes back," Lucas said. "Try it. Put the dot on your horizon line and send everything straight to it." He was already testing it further, sketching a food truck parked along the street, deciding whether to write CAMP CUISINE on the side or just leave it blank. A delivery van in the photo partially obstructed the view of a cabin, and he puzzled over that too, realizing that even the van's roofline and wheel edges had to obey the same rule, that everything, near or far, aimed at that one small point.

Mr. Grewal circled the room, pausing behind Lucas long enough to look but saying nothing, which Lucas took as a good sign. Mia glanced over at his new version and then, to his surprise, erased a whole corner of her own drawing and started again. "Mine was off," she admitted. "My street curved. A street in one-point perspective goes straight back."

"Dead straight," Lucas said, and ruled one more line from the dot to the corner of the page.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: One-point perspective works when you face straight down a street, so the fronts of objects face you and everything else recedes to one point.
story:
Elijah slid his sketchbook across the art room table so Soren and Lux could see the disaster. "Mr. Augustin says it needs a vanishing point. What even is that?"

"Where all the lines run into," Lux said, tapping the edge of his page. "Watch. You draw a dot, then every line of the street goes straight into it."

Elijah tried it right there. He set the dot low in the middle of the page and ran the curbs toward it, then the roofline of the corner store, then the power lines. The street actually looked like a street, deep and real, and he grinned so wide his face hurt. "Okay, that is the coolest thing I have ever drawn."

"Then collaborate with me on mine," Soren said, shoving his own sketchbook over. "Mine looks like a toxic spill." Soren's street was green and wobbly and, somehow, sideways.

On Saturday, Elijah took his sketchbook downtown to practice. He found a spot at the corner of Maple and Third, right beside the bait shop with the old fishing boat parked out front, its gray hull catching the morning light. Perfect subject. He drew the bait shop facing him, big and square, then started the side of the building going down Third Street toward a dot. It looked wrong. He tried the dot higher, then lower, then closer. Still wrong. The wall slanted like it was melting.

Lux had biked past and doubled back when she saw him frowning at the page. "What's the matter?"

"Look at this. It worked in the art room when we made up the street. It's broken out here."

Lux walked into the middle of the intersection, looked both ways, and stood still. "Come stand here."

He stood where she pointed, and the whole street snapped into place. The bait shop had its flat front staring right at him, and everything else, the sidewalks, the wires, the shop fronts stepping away, ran together toward one point far down the road.

"Oh," Elijah said. "You have to be facing straight down the street. That's the whole trick. From the corner you're looking at two different ways at once, so one dot can't hold it."

He sat down right in the crosswalk and drew fast, the boat's hull, the bait shop front flat and bold, every other line racing toward that single distant dot. "Lux, this is going to be the best thing anyone has ever put up on the art room wall."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Two people can agree on every fact about an event and still interpret it differently because they value different things, such as fairness versus loyalty.
story:
Livia burst into the art room at the community centre and found Karen and Margot standing on opposite sides of the paint cart, arms crossed. Both of them started talking at once, so she held up a hand and made them go one at a time, because the mural club had four days left to finish the wall by the gym, and they were the only two people who could still reach the high scaffolding.

The story came out in pieces. Last Saturday, Margot's friend had knocked over a jar of turquoise paint on the gym floor and left without telling anyone, and Margot had cleaned it up and said nothing. On Monday the coach had blamed the mess on the Saturday basketball kids, who lost their open-gym time because of it. Karen had found out yesterday and told Mr. Visser the truth. Margot was now saying Karen had betrayed her friend; Karen was saying Margot had let innocent kids take the blame. Both of them, Livia realized with a strange jolt, agreed on every single fact. Same jar, same mess, same lie, same consequence. They only disagreed about whether Karen had done right.

"You despise my friend, that's all this is," Margot said.

"I don't despise anyone," Karen shot back. "Those basketball players were endangered by staying quiet. Somebody had to speak up."

Livia dragged a stool between them and sat down. She had been reading about how her grandfather and his neighbour could look at the same old fence and argue about it for years, one seeing property, the other seeing history. Maybe this was like that. She tested it out loud. "Quick. Margot, tell me one fact we don't all agree on." Margot opened her mouth, then closed it. Karen tried too and shook her head. "See? There isn't one. We all agree what happened. You just care about different things." She pointed at Margot. "You're protecting loyalty." She pointed at Karen. "You're protecting fairness. That's the whole fight."

Neither of them answered for a second. Then Margot said, quietly, "I still think I was right to cover for her."

"And I'd do it again tomorrow," Karen said, and then, weirdly, both of them laughed, because they finally understood what they were actually arguing about.

Mr. Visser poked his head in and said the mural deadline had just been moved up two days, so the three of them would have to work side by side on the scaffolding whether they liked it or not. Margot picked up the turquoise and offered Karen the first brush, since she'd been the one to report the spill in the first place. "Your paint, your turn," she said.

Karen stared at it. "That's the exact colour I was going to say we should throw out."

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: Current measured in milliamps must be changed into amps before using Ohm's law; 250 milliamps is 0.25 amps.
story:
The science lab smelled like warm dust and old rubber, and the afternoon sun made the glossy counters shine. Avery clipped a thin copper wire into the circuit and watched the numbers settle on the multimeter: 3 volts, 250 on the current display. She wrote both numbers in her notebook and divided, because Ms. Lavoie had said resistance was voltage divided by current, and Ohm's law was supposed to be the easy part.

Her answer came out as 0.012. She frowned at it. Across the table, Alvin was busy drawing a diagram of their setup, and David was trying to read the tiny label on the spool of nichrome wire, holding it almost against his nose.

"That can't be right," Avery said. She swapped in a much thinner wire, the kind that should have resisted more, and measured again. 3 volts, 90 on the current display. She divided and got 0.033. The thin wire had less resistance than the thick one, which was backwards, and she knew it was backwards because they had tested the same two wires yesterday with the school's bigger meters and gotten completely different numbers.

She stared at the multimeter. The display was a hard, opaque little window, showing digits without telling her anything about them. Then she tipped it toward the light and found a small word printed above the readout: mA. Milliamps. Not amps.

"Alvin," she said slowly, "what if current measured in milliamps has to be changed into amps before you use Ohm's law?" She tried it with the numbers she had. Two hundred fifty milliamps had to be 0.25 amps, so 3 divided by 0.25 gave 12. For the thin wire, 90 milliamps would be 0.09 amps, and 3 divided by that gave 33.33. Big wire, small number. Thin wire, big number. The pattern flipped the right way around at last.

David leaned over her notebook. "So yesterday we were dividing by numbers a thousand times too big, and our answers came out a thousand times too small."

"Every single one," Avery said. She felt her conscience give a small twist, because the graph they had handed in on Monday was built on those wrong numbers. It was only homework, but it was wrong, and now she knew it.

She raised her hand before she could talk herself out of it. "Ms. Lavoie, our Monday graph has a mistake. We used the milliamp numbers like they were amps."

Ms. Lavoie came over, looked at the notebook page, and did something unexpected. She smiled. "Then you're the third group to catch it this week," she said. "Everyone who used the small multimeters made the same error. Fix your graph and tape it to the back, please."

Alvin groaned, but Avery was already copying the page over, her pencil steady, the corrected numbers marching down the paper in a neat column. David slid the spool of nichrome toward her.

"So," he said, "want to decompose the problem? One wire at a time, thin to thick?"

Avery picked up the clamps. "Start at the skinny end."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
