story:
The microphone smelled like pencil shavings, and Vincent's word was "citation," which meant he had to spell a word about words. He got it right, and the buzzer stayed silent, and Rayan clapped so hard the girl in front of him turned around.

Three rounds later it was down to Vincent and Alejandro. Alejandro spelled "conceal" without blinking, hiding the word inside himself like he'd done it a hundred times before. Then it was Vincent's turn again. "Lush," said Mr. Islam from the judge's table. "Lush. L-U-S-H. Lush." The bell didn't ring. Neither of them had missed a word since the opening round, and the audience had gone quiet in a bored, restless way, like they were waiting for someone to fail.

Vincent stared at the exit sign above the back doors and thought. He had read a whole article about the national bee last summer, one he'd mostly concealed from his friends because he didn't want them to know how much he cared. One detail had stuck with him: the 2019 Scripps National Spelling Bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right. Eight kids, one trophy, nobody second. He had thought it sounded like a disaster at the time. Now it sounded like a door.

Round after round, the pronouncer worked deeper into her list. She gave Alejandro "rigueur," and Vincent "verboten," and both of them spelled through, dry-mouthed, while the clock on the wall crawled. Vincent tested his idea in his head. If he kept spelling correctly, the bee could not end with him losing. It could only end with him winning, or with the words running out first. Both of those were better than second place. So the plan was simple: never miss.

The pronouncer checked her card, then checked it again, and leaned toward Mr. Islam. They whispered. Mr. Islam stood up. "We have exhausted the championship word list for this round," he announced. "The bee will conclude with two co-champions."

Alejandro's head snapped toward Vincent, and Vincent grinned back at him, sudden and wide. The two of them stood there under the hot lights while the audience came apart into cheering. "Tie?" Alejandro said, still gripping the microphone like he might have to spell one more. "Tie," Vincent said, and shook his hand.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: Foreshadowing is a hint early in a story about something that will happen later, often noticed only on a second reading.
story:
The rain hammered on the tin roof of his grandfather's house, so John spread his English homework across the kitchen table and stared at it. Ms. Baptiste had assigned a short story called "The Tropical Storm" and three questions, and tomorrow's class would be a discussion, not a quiz. John wanted to say something in that discussion that made Henrik and Marc-Antoine stop smirking for once. The problem was the third question: identify the foreshadowing and explain what it suggests. He had read the story twice and still could not find it.

His grandfather set down a cup of tea and looked over John's shoulder. "When I was a boy, we read this one in school," he said. "The storm in it, the big one on the last page. Read me the first page again, slow."

John read aloud. A boy in the story notices his mother nailing shutters closed while the sky is still blue. At the time John had skipped past it, because the weather seemed fine. He stopped and put his finger on the sentence. "She's boarding up the windows," he said. "But the storm doesn't arrive until the end. Why would the writer put that on page one?"

"Turn back through the pages," his grandfather said, "and count how many small things come before the storm."

John flipped backward. The shutters preceded the wind. A radio mentioned a ship changing course before anyone said the word hurricane. A dog refused to go to the beach a full scene before the waves rose. Each hint sat quietly in its paragraph, easy to miss the first time, obvious now that he knew the ending. He wrote the three clues in his notebook, then stopped, tapping his pencil. "But Ms. Baptiste wants what they suggest, not just what they are."

"So follow the logic," his grandfather said. "If the mother acts early, what does that tell you about her?"

John looked at the page again. The mother knew the storm was coming before the boy did. So the hints were not just about weather. They suggested that the adults in the story understood danger long before the child did, and the whole last page, where the boy finally listens to her, was being set up from the very first paragraph. He wrote it down, then crossed out half of it and wrote it again, tighter.

His phone buzzed. Marc-Antoine had texted the group: "Question 3 is impossible, I'm writing that there's no foreshadowing in this story." Henrik replied with a single crying-laughing face.

John typed back: "Page one. The shutters. Read it again, the whole first page, slowly." Then he underlined his answer one more time, closed the notebook, and carried his empty teacup to the sink while the rain kept drumming on the roof.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: One of the first written guides to online manners, 'Netiquette Guidelines', was published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855.
story:
The group chat for Ms. Wu's science project had existed for exactly four hours, and it was already a disaster. Grace scrolled up through forty-one messages, most of them from Elie, who had discovered the cat-with-sunglasses sticker and used it eleven times. Somebody had posted the lab data as a photo taken at an angle so steep it looked like abstract art. Then Gabriela had typed, "whatever, do it your way then," which sat on the screen like a smell nobody would name.

Grace wanted one thing: a chat that actually helped them finish the project before Friday. She typed, "Can we make some rules for this chat?" and immediately deleted it, because it sounded like she was running for hall monitor. She tried again. "Serious question, did anyone ever write official rules for how to act online? Like real ones?" Elie replied with the cat sticker. Gabriela replied, "idk maybe??"

She searched on her laptop, expecting cartoon posters about being kind. Instead she found something called RFC 1855, published in 1995, titled "Netiquette Guidelines." She read parts of it twice, partly because it was useful and partly because it was funny that adults in 1995 had sat around typing rules like it was homework. She screenshotted the title.

"Guess what," she posted. "There's an actual document. It's called 'Netiquette Guidelines,' from 1995." Elie sent three question marks. "It's numbered," Grace added. "RFC 1855. People wrote manners for the internet before I was born."

Gabriela typed, "so we have to follow it?" and then, before Grace could answer, "is it mandatory lol." Grace said no, but the document gave her an idea. Instead of announcing rules herself, she could copy the old ones and see if the group would cooperate. She picked three: don't post when you're angry, don't spam, and if you disagree, do it privately, not in front of everyone. She posted them as a poll: "Approve these as chat rules? Yes or no."

Elie voted yes within seconds, then added, "i vote no on the cat sticker ban though." There was no cat sticker ban, but Grace let that go. The poll closed with three yes votes, and the chat went quiet in a way that felt like people actually working. Grace sent the data as a clean list instead of the slanted photo, and Gabriela replied, "ok that's better, thanks."

At ten that night, a single message appeared from Gabriela: "hey, sorry about the 'whatever' earlier. bad day. elie sent me 6 cats so i think we're good." Grace read it twice, then went back to her notes. She had underlined one line from the 1995 document: "be conservative in what you send." She added, in her own handwriting, "and in what you take personally," then closed the laptop and turned off the lamp.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The bandwagon technique urges people to do or buy something because "everyone else is," appealing to the wish to belong rather than giving a reason.
story:
The group chat lit up at 7:42 on Tuesday night, and by 7:50 Madison's phone had buzzed eleven times. It was Kameron, posting screenshot after screenshot of a sneaker ad. "EVERYONE is getting the Vortex Plus," he typed. "Join the millions who already switched. Even Dex Halloran wears them." Alessandra replied with three fire emojis. Madison typed back, "what's better about them tho," and watched the typing dots appear and vanish twice before Kameron answered, "they just are. everyone has them."

Madison wanted them too. That was the trouble. She set the phone face-down on her desk, but the glow through the case was like a porch light and she was a moth. Her allowance was thirty-eight dollars and the shoes were ninety. She picked the phone up again. The ad filled her screen: a photo of Dex Halloran mid-jump, and under it, in bold letters, "The millions who switched can't be wrong."

She scrolled down looking for a single fact about the shoe. Cushioning? Grip? Durability? Nothing. The whole ad was other people. She got a piece of paper and wrote down every claim the ad made, then read the list back. Everyone is getting them. Millions switched. Dex Halloran wears them. Not one word about the shoe itself. She felt something click, the same click she got when she found the pattern in a math puzzle.

The next morning she showed her list to Alessandra at the lockers. "Notice anything?" Alessandra squinted at it. "It's all... people?" "Right. It wants you to buy them because everyone else is, not because they're better. It's going for wanting to belong." Ms. Wright, unlocking the classroom door, glanced over. "That's called the bandwagon technique," she said, and went inside. Madison wrote it at the top of her list.

To verify her idea, she ran a test. In the group chat she posted: "Saw Dex Halloran eats at the diner on Fifth. Everyone's going Thursday." Within two minutes Alessandra had replied "I'M IN" and Kameron had replied "obviously." Then Madison posted the follow-up: "Made that up. Why did you say yes?" Silence. Then Kameron: "because you said everyone was going." Then Alessandra: "ok that's embarrassing."

She sent one last message, a screenshot of the sneaker ad with the claims circled in red. "They never said what the shoe does. Only that everyone bought it. If it's actually better, the ad would just say so." The chat went quiet for a long time. That afternoon Kameron walked into class in his old sneakers, and when Madison raised an eyebrow at them, he shrugged and said, "They still fit."

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Glow sticks light up when bending breaks a glass vial of hydrogen peroxide inside, letting it mix with other chemicals and a dye in a reaction called chemiluminescence.
story:
Addison stood in the school parking lot between the parked cars and the gym doors, holding a paper bag of glow stick bracelets her mom had bought for the dance. The problem was that half of them had gone dark on the drive over, or maybe they had never worked at all. The dance started in eleven minutes, and Eleni was already at the doors, waving her inside.

"Addison, hurry up, they're playing the good song first!" Eleni called.

Addison held the bag up to the streetlight and shook it gently. Nothing glowed. She tried to think like a detective, the way Ms. Horváth was always nagging them to do. She sorted the bracelets into two piles on the hood of a nearby car, careful to keep the symmetry of the piles even, because crooked piles annoyed her. Pile one: bracelets that glowed faintly. Pile two: bracelets that were completely dead. "The dead ones feel stiff," she said aloud. "The other ones feel like there's liquid sloshing."

Eleni jogged over. "What are you doing, bracelet surgery?"

"Testing something." Addison picked up a glowing bracelet and a dead one. "When I bent the working ones in the car, they lit up. The dead ones didn't. So maybe something inside breaks when you bend them." She bent the glowing one again, sharper this time, and watched the light brighten and spread along the whole tube.

"That's it," said Ellen, who had appeared beside them with a backpack full of hairbrushes and, inexplicably, a rubber duck. "My cousin told me. Glow sticks light up when bending breaks a glass vial of hydrogen peroxide inside, letting it mix with other chemicals and a dye."

"There's a tiny glass tube in there?" Eleni said, holding a bracelet up to her eye like a jeweler. "In this? I've been wearing chemistry on my wrist all night?"

"It's called chemiluminescence," Ellen said. "I memorized it for a trivia contest. It's the only word I know with that many syllables, and I plan to use it."

Addison grinned and bent every bracelet in the good pile, one at a time, listening for the faint crack of the little vial. A few stayed stubbornly dark, and she set those aside. "Okay, new plan. We prioritize the ones that actually work. Ellen, you hold the good pile. Eleni, guard the duck."

"Why do you have a duck?" Eleni asked, but she took it anyway and perched it on a side mirror like a tiny, judgmental principal.

The gym doors swung open, spilling out music and purple light. Addison slid a cracked bracelet onto her wrist, watched it bloom bright green, and led the charge across the parking lot, three girls and one duck, glowing all the way to the doors.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Chinese, the word for 'four' sounds very similar to the word for 'death', so some buildings in East Asia skip the fourth floor.
story:
William stood in the lobby of the Lakeside apartments holding a box of pears, because his mother had said you never visit Ms. Koné empty-handed. Makenna from his science class lived on the eighth floor, and Ms. Koné was her great-aunt, and tonight there would be dumplings. He pressed the elevator button and watched the doors shudder open, trying to look like someone who was invited to eighth-floor apartments all the time.

Inside, Makenna jabbed the button marked five before he even stepped in. "We go up a lot," she said, which struck him as an odd thing to say about an elevator. As they rose, he counted the numbers lighting above the door. Three, then five, with nothing in between. He pressed his finger against the panel where four should have been. It was smooth metal, blank as a wall. "Your building's missing a floor," he said.

Makenna laughed. "No, it's not. Look, the button for four sounds like death in Chinese, so a lot of buildings skip it." She said it the way she'd say the sky was blue, and then the doors opened on five, which he now suspected was secretly the fifth floor no matter what the lobby claimed. He filed the idea away and followed her down the hall, where Ms. Koné waited with both hands folded in front of her, bowing slightly. William had almost stuck out his hand. At his grandmother's house back when he was nine, he remembered, you shook hands at the door, firm grip, eye contact, and he'd once gotten a lecture in the car about a limp handshake. Here he bowed back, a little too deep, and Ms. Koné's whole face crinkled with delight.

He held out the pears with both hands, and she took them with both hands and set them, unopened, on a shelf by the door. That nearly undid him. At his birthday parties, everyone tore wrapping paper the second it touched their laps; his cousin Theodore once opened a gift so fast he shredded the card inside. But he said nothing, because the premise of the evening seemed to be that you watched first and copied second. At dinner, he watched too. Chopsticks went on the little rest beside his bowl, never standing upright in the rice, and when Ms. Koné ladled soup into his bowl, he held it with both palms rather than one, because Makenna did.

"I counted the floors," he told her between dumplings. "From the outside. Your building has twelve stories, but the buttons only go to eleven, because four is gone." He had tested it that afternoon, standing in the parking lot, ticking off balconies with his eyes while the December wind tried to submerge his hands in his sleeves. Ms. Koné nodded like he had passed something.

"Very good," she said. "You are a careful boy."

He was still glowing about that on Monday, riding up to Theodore's tenth-floor apartment with a bag of leftover dumplings, ready to tell the whole story about the vanishing fourth floor. "Some buildings, the buttons skip four," Theodore said first, smugly, because his father worked in Singapore. "Guess what mine skips." The numbers climbed, nine, then eleven, and William looked at the blank panel and burst out laughing.

"Thirteen," Theodore said. "We live on it anyway."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Musical loudness is marked with Italian words: piano means soft and forte means loud.
story:
Alexis had one week to learn the middle section of "Night Ride" before Friday's band rehearsal, and the piece was fighting him. He sat at the upright piano in the music room after last bell, while the hallway outside emptied and the buses groaned away. The notes themselves were easy. The problem was the strange little letters scattered between the staff lines, letters like p and f and something with two f's, and every time he reached one, the music in his head fell apart.

"You're slamming that part," said Emerson, who had commuted across town on the late bus just to keep him company and was now lying under the xylophone like a napping bear. "The part with the little p. You play it like the piano owes you money."

Alexis looked at the page. "It's just a letter. Maybe it means pedal. Maybe it means push." He played the measure loud again, on purpose, and Emerson groaned from under the xylophone like a nocturnal creature dragged into daylight. Something about the letter kept snagging him. The piece was called "Night Ride," and the middle section was supposed to be the quiet part, the horse slipping through the dark. So why would the composer mark the quiet part with the same letter as loud playing? Unless it didn't mean loud at all. Unless p meant the opposite.

He tested it. He played the measure soft, barely touching the keys, letting the melody whisper. Then he hit the ff section and let it bloom. The music suddenly made sense, like a story with a narrator who leaned in close for the secret parts and threw his arms wide for the exciting ones. "It works," Alexis said. "The p parts are quiet. The f parts are loud. It's a code."

Madeleine wandered in from the choir room and peered over his shoulder. "That's Italian," she said. "Piano means soft, and forte means loud. Ms. Balogun has a poster about it on the door." She tapped the double f. "That one just means extra loud."

"Then why is the instrument called a piano?" Alexis asked, and Madeleine shrugged, and Emerson said, "Maybe it's short for something," and none of them solved it, which felt fine.

On Friday, Ms. Balogun counted them in, and Alexis rode the dynamics like they were hills, soft through the shadowy middle and full-voiced at the crest. Afterward she nodded once, and Madeleine grinned at him across the trombones, and Emerson gave him a thumbs-up from the percussion section. Alexis flipped the page to the next piece, saw a p in the third measure, and smiled at it like an old friend.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Raw onion tastes sharp, but cooking it slowly over low heat makes it soft and sweet as its natural sugars turn golden brown.
story:
Tristan stood at the kitchen counter with an onion in front of him and a promise behind him. His mom had agreed to a negotiation: if he made dinner sauce from scratch tonight, he could skip Saturday chores. He was willing to invest a whole afternoon in that deal, even if it meant learning to chop like Mr. Lau, the neighbour who ran the diner on the corner and had offered to teach him.

"Curl your fingertips under, like a claw," Mr. Lau said, guiding Tristan's hand. "The knuckles stick out and keep the blade away. The onion can't bite you if your fingers are tucked in." Tristan pressed down carefully, and the onion fell into pale pieces. He sniffed, then wrinkled his nose. A raw chunk went into his mouth before anyone could stop him, and he spat it into the trash. "That's the sharpest thing I've ever tasted."

His little sister Yuna wandered in, saw the cutting board, and backed toward the doorway. "I'm not eating those," she announced. "Onions are spicy and gross. I always pick them out."

"That's because you've only had them raw," Tristan said, remembering something Mr. Lau had muttered while setting the pan. "Watch." He slid the chopped onion into the pot and turned the burner down low, the way Mr. Lau had shown him, letting it sit and soften instead of rushing it. He was skeptical at first that anything so slow could matter, and he hovered over the pot, nudging the pieces around.

But after a while the kitchen began to smell different, warmer and almost like caramel. The onion pieces turned from white to a soft golden brown, going glossy and tender in the pan. Tristan fished one out with a spoon, blew on it, and held it out to Yuna. "One taste. If you hate it, you never have to touch an onion again. Deal?" Yuna eyed the spoon like it was a trap, then leaned in and took the smallest possible bite. Her eyebrows went up. She reached for the spoon again before he could say anything.

"More of the golden ones," she said, climbing onto a stool to see into the pot. "They're sweet."

Tristan stirred the crushed tomatoes into the onions, added a pinch of salt, and lowered the heat so the sauce could bubble gently while the pasta water came to a boil. Mr. Lau squeezed his shoulder on his way to the door. "Tomorrow you learn garlic," he said, and let himself out.

Later, at the table, Yuna held up her fork with a piece of onion balanced on it. "These are the good ones," she told their mom. "Tristan made them sweet."

"He made them golden," Tristan corrected her, ladling more sauce over her plate.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: The U.S. agency NIOSH recommends limiting exposure to 85 decibels to eight hours a day, and each 3-decibel increase halves the safe listening time.
story:
The car smelled like her mom's coffee and Lucy's borrowed perfume, and the radio was playing something random that nobody had chosen. Lucy checked her phone for the tenth time. "Lane and Subhan are already in line," she said. "Drive faster, but safely."

Her mom laughed. "It's your first dance, not a siege. You'll get there." But she did go a little faster, and when they pulled into the school lot Lucy saw the gym windows pulsing with colored light. Before she got out, her mom called, "Text me if the music's too loud! Your uncle ruined his ears at concerts!"

In the gym, the speakers stood taller than lockers, and Lucy found Lane and Subhan pressed right up against them, arms crossed, heads nodding. Her ears felt strange within a minute, a pressure like water in them. She opened a decibel meter app she'd downloaded after her mom's warning, because she wanted to test a rule she'd read: the U.S. agency NIOSH recommends limiting exposure to 85 decibels to eight hours a day, and each 3-decibel increase halves the safe listening time. Next to the speakers, the app read 112.

"Eighty-five is safe for eight hours," she shouted at Lane. "Every three decibels louder cuts that time in half." Lane's eyes went wide as she counted on her fingers. From eight hours it fell to four, then two, then one, down and down through the halvings until the number was smaller than the length of one song. Subhan grabbed both their sleeves. "Then we're standing in the worst possible spot," he yelled, and the three of them retreated across the gym until the meter read 88, which Lucy worked out to a safe stretch of hours, plenty for the whole night.

"The loud zone is like a circle around the speakers," Lane said, looking back at the crowd still packed against the wall of sound. "They don't even know." Lucy almost went to tell them, but the DJ played the song she and Lane had practiced to in her bedroom, simulating this exact moment a hundred times, and the problem of strangers' ears lost the fight. She and Lane ran to the middle of the floor, where Subhan was already dancing badly and proudly.

When her mom picked her up, Lucy's ears were fine, only ringing a little from the three encore songs. "Was it too loud?" her mom asked, pulling out of the lot. Lucy held up her phone with the meter still open. "The front was," she said. "We did the math."

fact: Oil paint does not dry by water evaporating; its oil slowly reacts with oxygen in the air, so an oil painting can take days or longer to dry to the touch.
story:
Vincent set the model tank on a spread of newspaper in the garage, his brush hovering. He had spent two evenings mixing greens and browns into a ragged camouflage pattern, and tonight he wanted the last layer done. Dominik's birthday was tomorrow, and the whole class was meeting at the park at four. He worked with quick, agile strokes, laying a stripe of olive along the turret, then sat back on the stool to wait for the paint to dry so he could wrap the thing.

After twenty minutes he touched the edge of the hull with one fingertip. It came away glossy. He wiped the smudge on his jeans and checked the clock on the wall. He had used the little tubes from the art box in the closet, the ones that said oil paint in small letters. His watercolors from school could dry before he finished washing a brush, and that difference nagged at him. If the water wasn't leaving these paints the way it left watercolors, then something else had to be going on.

He tried an experiment. In one corner of the newspaper he brushed a wet stripe of plain water mixed with a drop of brown watercolor, and beside it a stripe of the oil paint. The watercolor stripe went matte in a couple of minutes. The oil stripe stayed tacky and shining under the garage light. He tapped it, pressed it, even blew on it, which only fogged the paint. Whatever was happening, it wasn't water evaporating off the top.

He called Tanya, who kept her phone on the counter while she did dishes. "You know the oil paints your mom uses?" he asked. "Mine are still sticky after an hour."

"That's normal," she said. "Oil paint doesn't dry the way water does. The oil mixes with the oxygen in the air, slowly. Days sometimes, my mom says, before you can even touch it."

Vincent looked at the tank, then at the clock. "Days. Dominik's party is at four tomorrow."

"So don't touch it. Don't wrap it. Don't even sneeze near it."

He carried the tank upstairs with both hands, moving like a waiter with a full tray, and set it on his desk by the open window. He pushed every pencil and book to the far side so nothing could roll and demolish the wet camouflage. Then he texted his mom to drive carefully tomorrow, corners slow, because he would be riding with the tank flat on his lap, level as a tray of soup, all the way to the park.

In the morning the paint still shone faintly under his lamp, soft as toffee, and he laid a sheet of wax paper over nothing at all, just hovered it above the turret to see the pattern through the translucence. "Hold on," he told the tank. "You're riding with me."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Avoiding everything that causes anxiety brings quick relief but often makes the anxiety stronger over time, because the person never learns the situation is manageable.
story:
Stella had watched Leticia fake a cough through three English presentations in a row, and tonight, sprawled on Leticia's bedroom floor with math homework ignored, she decided to test a theory. "So what actually happens," she asked, "when you skip?"

Leticia shrugged from the bed. "Relief. Like a door closing. Mr. Kamau marks me absent for the day and I just read my part at home instead."

"That's the part I don't get. The first time, in September, you were shaking but you still stood up there. The second time you stayed in your seat. Now you don't even come to class on presentation days." Stella flipped her pencil over. "It's like the skipping isn't holding the door closed. It's making the thing behind the door bigger."

From the kitchen below came the clank of a wrench. Leticia's mom had finally called Mr. Kamau from next door to deal with the leaking plumbing, and he'd been at the pipes for an hour, muttering to himself in a way that made Stella want to laugh. "See, that's stress with a fix," Stella said, gesturing at the ceiling. "The pipe leaks, he shows up, it gets repaired. You can't send somebody into your head with a wrench."

"You think I don't know that?" Leticia pulled her pillow against her chest. Then she reached under the mattress and handed Stella a folded page, her handwriting cramped along the lines. It was a letter to Mr. Kamau, dated two weeks ago, explaining that she wasn't lazy, that she had anxiety, that she wanted to present alone after school where nobody could laugh. The letter had never been sent. The bottom edge was soft from being refolded so many times.

Stella read it twice. "This is good. Why is it under your mattress?"

"Because if I give it to him, he'll say yes. And then I'll have to actually do it."

"Okay," Stella said slowly, and she could feel the idea assembling itself out of everything she'd noticed since September. "But think about it backwards. Every time you skip, the next one feels worse, right? The relief lasts an hour and the fear lasts longer. So the skipping is feeding it." She tapped the letter. "The relief is the trap. If you go through it instead, you find out it's survivable, and then it's a little less next time." She hesitated, because the next part wasn't hers to decide. "I'm not saying stand up in front of everyone Monday. Send the letter. Do it alone with him first. That's still going through the door."

Leticia stared at the page for a long moment. "My mom says I need better coping. I thought coping meant avoiding the stuff that hurts." She laughed, a short, cracked sound. "I was excluding the one thing that would help."

They walked it over together, since Mr. Kamau was still downstairs fixing the sink, sleeves rolled up, water spots on his shirt. Leticia handed him the folded letter without a word. He read it, looked up at her, and said quietly, "Tuesday after school, then. Just us." On the way back upstairs Leticia's shoulders were somewhere near her ears, and Stella knew Tuesday was going to be awful anyway, that there was no version of this without the shaking hands and the hot face. But the letter was out of the mattress and into somebody's hands, and Leticia, who could be resilient about everything except this one thing, was maybe starting on that too. From below, the wrench clanked once more, and the pipe went quiet.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: When the brain senses a threat, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and breathing quicker. This is called the fight-or-flight response.
story:
Nathan's hands were shaking, and he had a theory about why. He stood in the wings of the school auditorium, third in line for the spring talent show, and watched his fingers tremble like he was holding a bug zapper. Adelaide had gone pale before her piano piece last year and sworn she was coming down with something. Then Mr. Iyer had asked her one question and fixed everything. Nathan had never found out what the question was, and tonight he needed it.

"Your heart's going like a drum solo," said Lillian, who was working the lights and had come over during a mic check. "You look terrible, honestly."

"I'm not sick," Nathan said, though he wasn't sure. "Okay, maybe. My heart's pounding and my breathing got all fast and weird."

Lillian grinned. "Adelaide had the exact same thing. I was there. Mr. Iyer asked her if she knew what happens when the brain senses a threat. The adrenal glands release adrenaline, and that makes your heart beat faster and your breathing quicker. He called it the fight-or-flight response."

Nathan stared at her. "My brain thinks the talent show is a bear?"

"A hundred and forty people in folding chairs, basically a bear," Lillian said.

So it wasn't a virus. It was a system, an invisible one, firing on purpose. That meant he could test it. If adrenaline was the hidden cause, then telling his body the threat was fake should intervene before the shaking got worse. He remembered the breathing trick from health class, the slow four-count, and tried it right there behind the curtain. In. Hold. Out. His heart kept drumming, but the sharp, panicky edge of it dulled a little. Interesting. It needed more than one try.

He ducked into the hallway and pulled out his phone. Adelaide had moved schools in October, but she still answered fast.

You onstage in 10, shaking like crazy, he typed. Did the breathing thing actually work for you, or did it take longer?

Her reply came in three bursts. It worked but not instantly, took me a few nights. The real fix was sleep. I used to stay up till 1 practicing and it made everything worse. Routine every night, same time, no screens. After a week the pounding barely showed up. PS you will be amazing.

Nathan filed that away as the long-term component of the plan and went back to the wings. Second act was finishing. The breathing, he decided, was the acute fix, the thing you grabbed in the moment, and the sleep was the training that made the moment smaller. He did another round of slow breaths, and when the MC called his name, his hands had gone from trembling to merely buzzing.

He walked out under Lillian's lights, heart still loud, and found that a loud heart could carry a song. He played, the applause cracked like thunder, and offstage Adelaide's message glowed on his screen: Told you.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller.
story:
When Alexander enrolled in the winter swim program at the community centre, he expected laps, flip turns, and maybe a relay or two. What he got on the first Friday was a thick rope stretched across the shallow end of the pool, with Mr. Zhang barking, "Tug-of-war in the water! It builds grip and it builds legs."

Alexander's team of six lost twice to Graham's team of six, even though Alexander was sure his side was stronger. He had watched Graham's bunch splash around all season, and his own team included Madeleine, who could do twenty pull-ups without blinking. Something did not add up, and he kept turning it over on the bus home. Was it footing? The wet tiles? Or were people not pulling as hard as they claimed?

The next practice, he ran a quiet experiment. He tied a small strip of coloured rubber from his goggles around the rope exactly one arm's length from Madeleine's hands, then stood where he could watch it. When six of them heaved together, the strip barely shivered under Madeleine's grip, as though her tendon-shortening, muscle-flexing pull had gone soft. Then Mr. Zhang split them into pairs, and the same strip snapped taut like a plucked guitar string. Same rope, same hands, wildly different pull. Alexander grinned so wide he swallowed a mouthful of chlorinated water.

He cornered Mr. Zhang by the kickboard rack. "Did we look lazy out there? Because I don't think anyone was faking." Mr. Zhang shook his head and said only, "Look up Ringelmann." That night, Alexander did. In 1913, Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller. Alexander read the sentence three times, then called Graham, because a discovery that good should not be kept to yourself.

"So we weren't slackers," Graham said over the phone. "We were normal."

"That's the weird part," Alexander said. "It happens to everybody. Even us, even when we think we're going all out." He wondered whether his own pull had shrunk too, hidden somewhere inside him where he could never watch it directly. Could you feel it happening? Could you fight it? There was only one way to find out.

At the next practice, Alexander asked Mr. Zhang to line them up again, but this time each person got their own separate rope end looped around a heavy drag bucket. Six pullers, six buckets, six foam trails churned white across the blue water. Madeleine's bucket shot ahead like a startled fish. "Now that," Alexander panted, hauling his own bucket toward the wall, "is what my pull looks like when nobody's hiding in it."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: The equals sign was invented by the Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in 1557, who chose two parallel lines because no two things could be more equal.
story:
Elizabeth had failed the last quiz, and her mother had responded by signing her up for Tuesday nights at the tutoring centre, which Elizabeth found tedious even before she walked in. Room four smelled of whiteboard marker. Haris was already there, copying problems like a machine. Odin slid into the seat beside her and whispered, "Miss anything?"

"Three weeks of quizzes," Elizabeth said. "All of them with x on them."

Ms. Goh wrote 3x + 4 = 19 on the board and told them to get x alone. Elizabeth stared at it. On the page, x was just a letter pretending to be a number, and she could not see what it was hiding. She guessed ten. Three tens plus four was thirty-four, not nineteen, so ten was wrong, and she crossed it out hard enough to tear a little.

"Try undoing it," Odin said. "Take the four off."

Elizabeth subtracted four. "3x = 15," she read, then stopped. "Wait. The other side. Do I have to do it there too?"

"If you don't, the equals sign is a lie," Odin said. He pointed at the two little parallel lines with his pen. "Haris knows who made that thing."

Haris looked up from his machine-copying. "Robert Recorde," he said. "A Welsh mathematician, 1557. He picked two parallel lines because no two things could be more equal."

"So if I subtract four from one side," Elizabeth said slowly, "the other side stays equal only if I subtract four there too. That's the whole rule?" She divided both sides by three and got x = 5. She tested it the way she'd tested ten, because she no longer trusted pages that hid things: three fives plus four made nineteen. The equals sign was not a lie. She sat back, surprised at herself.

Ms. Goh moved around the room, bending over Haris's page. "Haris, you've solved eight of these but you dropped the operation on the right side four times. The sign can't accommodate one-sided arithmetic."

"Propaganda," Haris muttered. "The sign has turned you all against me."

Ms. Goh put a new problem on the board, harder, with brackets, and Elizabeth pulled her page closer. First move: the four had to come off both sides. She wrote it, checked it, tested the answer against the original line. Then she raised her hand anyway, because she wanted the next one.

"Give me one with fractions," she said.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Pencil 'lead' has never contained the metal lead; the name comes from early writers mistaking graphite for a kind of lead ore.
story:
Mia had the whole dining table to herself, which almost never happened on a Saturday. She spread out her colored pencils, the fine liner pens, and the sheet of watercolor paper she had been saving for a portrait of her grandmother, done in the style of the old photographs from her family's heritage box on the shelf. Her little cousin Ben sat across from her, swinging his legs, because his mom was next door and he had decided Mia's project was more interesting than cartoons.

He was fine until Mia picked up her graphite pencil to sketch the first lines. Ben went pale and pushed his chair back.

"You're not supposed to touch that," he said. "Lead poison."

Mia laughed, then stopped, because he looked genuinely scared. "Wait, you think a pencil can poison you?" She turned the pencil over in her hand, wondering about it. Everyone called it lead, so where had that name even come from? She hadn't actually asked herself that before, and now it itched at her like a puzzle piece that didn't quite fit. If it were really lead, the metal, wouldn't there be warnings on the box?

"Prove it," Ben said, arms crossed. He was not going to be gullible twice in one week, not after Dana had convinced him that the school cafeteria meatloaf was made of octopus.

So Mia made it a project inside her project. She flipped her pencil and squinted at the tiny words stamped into the wood, but they only said a number and a brand. She fetched the tablet and typed carefully, monitoring Ben's face as the page loaded, the way she would watch a pot about to boil. The answer came up fast, and she read it aloud, grinning by the second sentence.

"It's called graphite," she said. "Pencil lead has never contained the metal lead. Not once, ever. The name got stuck on because early writers found the stuff and thought it was a kind of lead ore." She tapped the screen. "So people have been calling it lead for hundreds of years just because of a mix-up at the start."

Ben leaned over the tablet, reading the words himself, his bare feet still hooked on the chair rung. He looked from the screen to the pencil, then back, doing his own checking.

"Okay," he said finally. "Then draw her. But can I do the eyes?"

Mia slid a spare pencil across the table, and Ben got to work, tongue poking out, pressing so hard the tip snapped clean off. He held up the broken bit and examined the shiny gray core like a jeweler.

"It does look kind of like metal," he admitted.

"That's the ore part, probably," said Mia. "Don't eat it anyway."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: U.S. food safety guidelines say poultry is safely cooked when its thickest part reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, or about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer.
story:
Ethan slid the roasting pan into his grandfather's oven at exactly five o'clock, because the whole family would walk through the door at six thirty and Granddad, who had twisted his ankle that morning, was counting on him for dinner. His reputation as the kitchen kid had started two summers ago with pancakes, but tonight's menu was roast chicken, potatoes and carrots, and chicken felt like a bigger deal. "Nobody gets sick in this family on my watch," he said to himself, pulling the meat thermometer from the drawer.

Kristopher and Oskar had come over to help, though mostly they were watching and eating the carrots meant for the pan. "How do you know when it's done?" Oskar asked, leaning on the counter. "My dad just cuts it open and looks."

"That's guessing," Ethan said. He turned the thermometer in his hand. "There's a rule for this. Poultry is safely cooked when its thickest part reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a thermometer." He had read it on a food safety sheet Ms. Charles, the neighbour across the fence, had given him when she heard about the dinner plan.

"How do you find the thickest part without slicing the whole thing open?" Kristopher asked. Ethan thought about that. He couldn't see inside the chicken, but he could reason it out: the thickest part had to be up near the breast, where the meat piled highest, not the skinny drumsticks that would cook first. He tested his idea by probing the thick side, then a thin spot near a leg. The thin spot read 180 already. The breast read 148. So the drumsticks weren't the measure; the hidden center of the thickest piece was. "The outside lies," he muttered, closing the oven door. "The thermometer doesn't."

Oskar envied him the thermometer, and said so, and Ethan handed it over so Oskar could take the next reading himself. At six fifteen the breast finally read 166, and Ethan let out a breath. They piled the potatoes and carrots around the bird and set the table in a rush, Kristopher folding napkins into wobbly triangles while Oskar filled the water glasses without being asked, because he had noticed Granddad's ankle was propped on a pillow and getting up was hard for him.

When the family sat down, Granddad took one bite of chicken and raised his eyebrows. "Perfect," he said. "Not dry, not pink. How'd you manage it?" Ethan shrugged, but Oskar couldn't keep quiet. "He poked it with a science stick," he announced, and everyone laughed. Ms. Charles, who had been invited to join them, raised her glass of water. "To the boy with the thermometer," she said. Ethan grinned and passed his grandfather the potatoes first.
